title: You can smell rain on dry earth at under one part per billion
body: The earthy smell after a dry spell has a name, **petrichor**, coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists from the Greek for stone and for the fluid in the veins of the gods. Much of it is geosmin, a compound made by soil bacteria called Streptomyces, which our noses detect at well under a part per billion. Rain doesn’t create the smell: it releases oils and geosmin that built up in dry soil and flings them into the air.

slides.alt: A raindrop lands on soil, trapping air bubbles that burst into tiny droplets, which rise carrying geosmin and plant oils.
slides.caption: Raindrops trap air, and the bursting bubbles launch the scent.

slides.label: the level of geosmin, an earthy compound made by soil bacteria, that a nose can detect
slides.text: Estimates range from about 5 to 400 parts per trillion. At the low end, that is less than a single drop in an Olympic swimming pool.

slides.heading: What’s in the smell
items: Geosmin, made by Streptomyces bacteria living in the soil
Oils that plants shed in dry weather, which collect on rock and soil
Air: a 2015 study filmed raindrops trapping bubbles that burst into scent-carrying droplets

slides.heading: Why bacteria bother
slides.text: Geosmin isn’t for us. Springtails, tiny soil creatures, are drawn to it, feed on the Streptomyces and carry its spores to new ground. The smell is advertising, and we just happen to be very good at reading it.

And carry its spores to new ground

slides.question: Which of these makes the earthy part of the smell of rain?
slides.explanation: Streptomyces bacteria in the soil make geosmin, and rain flings it into the air along with oils that plants shed in dry weather.

slides.clue: The name for the smell of rain on dry earth, coined in 1964 from the Greek for stone and for the gods’ blood
slides.detail: From petra, stone, and ichor, the fluid said to run in the veins of the Greek gods. Two Australian scientists coined it in 1964.
